This can be a frustrating and potentially dangerous situation. Please prioritize safety first. If you smell burning, see smoke, or if the dryer feels excessively hot to the touch, unplug it immediately or turn off the circuit breaker. Do not wait for it to finish its cycle.

If there is no immediate fire hazard but the dryer simply won’t stop running (or continues tumbling/running after the cycle ends), here are the most common causes and troubleshooting steps:

### 1. Check the Control Panel
• Stuck Buttons: Sometimes buttons can get stuck or sticky (especially if you’ve spilled something). Try pressing all buttons firmly to ensure they aren’t physically depressed.
• Child Lock: Some models have a child lock feature that may be interfering with controls. Consult your manual to see how to disable it.
• Power Cycle: Unplug the dryer for 5–10 minutes, then plug it back in. This can reset the electronic control board if it’s glitching.

### 2. Faulty Timer or Electronic Control Board
• Mechanical Timers (older models): If you have a dial-style timer, the internal mechanism may be worn out or stuck in the "on" position. You may hear clicking sounds as it tries to advance but fails. This usually requires replacement of the timer.
• Electronic Controls (newer models): The main control board may have failed. If buttons are unresponsive or the display is frozen, this is likely the culprit.

### 3. Door Switch Issue
• Most dryers will not run if the door isn’t closed properly. However, a faulty door switch can sometimes send incorrect signals to the control board, causing it to ignore stop commands. Try opening and closing the door firmly several times to see if it resets. If you hear a distinct "click" when closing the door, the switch may be working; if not, it might need replacement.

### 4. Thermal Fuse or High-Limit Thermostat (Safety Shutoff)
• While these usually cause a dryer not to start, in rare cases, a shorted thermostat can send continuous power to the motor. If your dryer is overheating, this is critical. Check if the lint filter and vent hose are clogged. A blocked vent causes overheating, which can damage internal components.

### 5. Relay or Motor Control Issue
• Inside the dryer, a relay on the control board may be stuck in the "closed" position, sending continuous power to the motor even when you press stop. This often happens after a power surge or due to age.

---

### What You Should Do Now:
1. Unplug the dryer if it’s still running and you can’t stop it manually via controls.
2. Check for clogs: Inspect the lint filter, exhaust vent hose, and exterior vent flap. A severely blocked vent is a fire hazard and can cause operational issues.
3. Reset power: Unplug for 5–10 minutes, then plug back in. Test if it stops when you press "Stop" or "Cancel."
4. Consult your manual: Look up the specific model number for error codes or known issues.
5. Call a professional: If the problem persists after resetting and checking vents, the issue is likely internal (timer, control board, or relay). These require disassembly and electrical work. Do not attempt to repair internal wiring unless you are qualified.

### ⚠️ Important Safety Note:
A dryer that won’t stop can overheat, leading to a fire risk. If you cannot resolve the issue quickly by unplugging it, leave the house if you smell burning and call emergency services or a professional appliance repair technician immediately.
its not hot and no smell. it just turns for a few seconds every couple of minutes after it says End. stops if i open the door

This specific behavior—running briefly every few minutes after the cycle ends, but stopping when the door is opened—is actually normal operation for most modern dryers. It is not a malfunction.

Here’s what is happening:

### 1. The "End" Signal vs. Motor Power
When your dryer displays "End," it means the heating element has turned off and the timed cycle is complete. However, many dryers are designed to keep the drum tumbling for a short period after the heat stops. This helps prevent wrinkles from setting in while you’re still nearby or just finishing up laundry.

### 2. The "Anti-Settling" or "Refresh" Cycle
The brief bursts of tumbling every few minutes are likely part of an anti-wrinkle or refresh feature. The dryer’s control board periodically tumbles the drum to keep clothes loose and prevent them from settling into creases while they sit in the drum. This is common in both mechanical-timer and electronic-control models.

### 3. Door Switch Safety Feature
The fact that it stops when you open the door confirms your door switch is working correctly. The dryer’s safety design requires the motor to stop whenever the door is opened, regardless of whether the cycle is "on" or in this post-cycle refresh mode. This prevents injury and ensures the drum doesn’t spin while you’re loading/unloading.

### What You Can Do:
• Leave it alone: If there’s no heat, no noise beyond normal tumbling, and no error codes, this is safe and intended behavior. The dryer will eventually stop completely if left undisturbed for 15–30 minutes.
• Remove your laundry: Take your clothes out as soon as the "End" signal appears to avoid any minor wrinkling from the post-cycle tumbling.
• Check your manual: Look for features like "Wrinkle Care," "Anti-Crease," or "Refresh Cycle." Your model likely has this enabled by default.

### When to Worry:
You should only be concerned if:
• The drum continues to tumble for hours after the cycle ends (e.g., overnight).
• You hear unusual grinding, squealing, or buzzing noises during these brief tumbles.
• The dryer starts heating again unexpectedly after displaying "End."

Since your dryer is cool and odorless, this is almost certainly just a normal feature to keep clothes fresh until you remove them.
ok but it carries on for about an hour if i leave it. is it wasting electricity?

Yes, technically it is using a small amount of electricity, but it’s likely negligible in cost. Here’s why:

### 1. The Motor Uses Very Little Power
The drum motor in a dryer typically draws between 0.5 to 1.5 amps at 240 volts (in North America) or 230–240V (elsewhere). This translates to roughly 120–360 watts.

• If the motor runs intermittently for an hour, it might only run for a few minutes total during that time.
• At 300 watts for just 5 minutes of actual running time, you’re using about 0.025 kWh (kilowatt-hours).
• At an average electricity rate of $0.15/kWh, this costs less than $0.004 (less than half a cent) per cycle.

### 2. No Heat = Low Energy Use
Since the heating element is off (as indicated by the "End" signal and no heat), you’re only powering the motor and possibly some small control board lights or sensors. The vast majority of a dryer’s energy use comes from the heater, which is not active here.

### 3. Why It Runs for an Hour
Some dryers have a built-in timer for their "anti-wrinkle" or "refresh" mode that lasts up to 60–90 minutes after the cycle ends. This is designed to give you time to unload laundry without it settling into permanent creases.

### Recommendation:
• Unplug it or turn off the breaker if you want to stop it immediately and save any energy (though, as shown, the savings are tiny).
• Leave it alone if convenience matters more than a fraction of a cent. It’s safe and won’t damage your clothes or dryer.

### If You Want to Disable This Feature:
Check your user manual for options like:
• "Wrinkle Care": May be adjustable or turn-off-able in settings.
• Timer Models: Some mechanical timers have a "Cool Down" period that can’t be adjusted, but you can manually stop it by turning the dial to "Off."

In short: It’s wasting a tiny amount of electricity (likely less than $0.01 per cycle), but it’s not harmful or expensive.
ok. my manual says something but i havent read it. how do i stop it doing that?

Since you haven’t read the manual yet, here are the most common ways to disable the post-cycle tumbling (often called "Wrinkle Care," "Anti-Crease," or "Refresh") depending on your dryer type:

### 1. For Electronic Control Models (Digital Display)
• Look for a Button: Check if there’s a button labeled "Wrinkle Care," "Anti-Crease," "Refresh," or "Extra Dry." Pressing it may toggle the feature off.
• Hold to Disable: Some models require you to hold down a specific button (like "Time Dry" or "Temp") for 3–5 seconds to enter settings mode, where you can turn Wrinkle Care on/off.
• Check Settings Menu: If your dryer has a "Settings" or "Options" menu, navigate to it and look for an option to disable post-cycle tumbling.

### 2. For Mechanical Timer Models (Dial)
• Turn Dial Fully Off: Ensure the timer dial is turned completely past the "End" position to "Off." Some older models will continue to tumble until you manually turn the knob all the way off.
• No Disable Option: Many mechanical dryers do not have a way to disable this feature. It’s hardwired into the timer mechanism.

### 3. Universal Quick Fix
• Unplug or Flip Breaker: If you can’t find the setting, simply unplug the dryer or turn off its circuit breaker as soon as the "End" signal appears. This is the most reliable way to stop it immediately.

### Recommendation:
1. Check for a "Wrinkle Care" button on your control panel first.
2. If you have an electronic model, look in the settings menu.
3. If that fails, unplug it or flip the breaker when the cycle ends. It’s safe and stops the feature instantly.

its a Beko. i dont know the model number, where do i look? i dont have a wrinkle button that i can see

To find your Beko dryer’s model number, check these locations:

1. Inside the door frame – Look on the metal edge of the door opening or on the door itself (sometimes on a sticker).
2. Behind the lint filter – Remove the lint filter and look inside the cavity for a label.
3. On the back or side – Check the rear panel or sides near the power cord entry.
4. Under the top lid – If it’s a front-load dryer, lift the top cover (may require removing screws) to find a sticker underneath.

The model number usually starts with letters like "DUE," "DUO," "BWD," etc., followed by numbers and sometimes a suffix like "-W" or "-T."

Once you have it, I can give you exact steps to disable the post-cycle tumbling!
ok i'll go and look. is it the door recess bit? will let you know what it says

Yes, check the metal frame around the opening where the door seals (the door recess). Look for a white or silver sticker with "Model:" followed by letters and numbers. If you don’t see it there, also check behind the lint filter inside the drum cavity. Let me know what it says!
i had a look but i'm not sure which bit is the model number, sorry. is there another way to stop it?

No problem! If you can’t find the model number, here are some universal ways to stop the post-cycle tumbling on most dryers:

### 1. Turn Off at the Wall or Breaker
The most reliable method:
• Unplug the dryer from the wall outlet as soon as it says "End."
• Or flip off the dedicated circuit breaker for the dryer in your electrical panel. This completely cuts power and stops any further tumbling.

### 2. Check for a Hidden Setting
Some Beko models hide settings behind button combinations:
• Try holding down the "Time Dry" or "Start/Pause" button for 5–10 seconds after the cycle ends.
• Look for small buttons labeled "Options," "Settings," or an icon that looks like a gear ⚙️ on your control panel.

### 3. Manual Stop
If your dryer has a mechanical dial:
• Turn it fully clockwise past "End" to the "Off" position. This should cut power to the motor.

### 4. Accept It as Normal
As mentioned earlier, this feature is designed to prevent wrinkles and uses very little electricity (less than $0.01 per cycle). If you’re okay with that tiny cost, you can leave it running—it’s safe and won’t damage your dryer or clothes.

ok. my manual says something about it but i havent read it. should i look in there?

Yes, absolutely! The manual is the best place to find the exact steps for your specific model. Here’s how to get started:

1. Find the Manual Online
   • Go to Beko’s official website or a trusted site like ManualsLib.com.
   • Search using any numbers/letters you can see on your dryer (even partial ones).
   • Look for sections titled “Wrinkle Care,” “Anti-Crease,” “Refresh Mode,” or “Post-Cycle Tumbling.”

2. What to Look For in the Manual
   • How to disable the feature via button combinations.
   • Whether it’s adjustable (e.g., 15, 30, or 60 minutes).
   • If there’s a specific setting menu to turn it off completely.

3. Quick Tip While You Search
   If you can’t find the manual right away, just unplug the dryer or flip its breaker when the cycle ends. It’s safe and stops the feature instantly.
